explanations.explanation: Mary Magdalene it is, friend. Mark says Jesus “…appeared first to Mary Magdalene…” (Mark 16:9). She's the one He had driven seven demons out of, and she's the first to see Him risen. I think that makes her morning pretty hard to top.

Simon Peter is a fair name to guess, so I see why he came to mind. But verse 9 puts someone else at the front of the line, and that's Mary Magdalene. Mark says “first,” and the order matters. Peter just isn't the name in this spot.

Joseph of Arimathea was a member of the Council who asked for Jesus' body after He died (Mark 15:43). He's a real part of the story, but that part came earlier. On the first day of the week, Mark says Jesus “…appeared first to Mary Magdalene…” Joseph is in the story, just not in this line.

She doesn't keep it to herself. Verse 10 says, “She went and told those who had been with Him…” Seeing the risen Jesus and then sitting on it? I can't even keep a fresh batch quiet for ten minutes, and cookies are way smaller news.
Right, false. Mary sees Jesus, and then she goes and tells people. Mark 16:10 says, “She went and told those who had been with Him…” News like that has a way of leaving the building.

Mourning is the word Mark uses. The people who had been with Jesus were “…mourning and weeping.” (Mark 16:10). So Mary is carrying the biggest news there is to people in tears. I think that's a hard moment to bring news into.
Praying sounds like a fair guess for sad people. But verse 10 says they were “…mourning and weeping.” That's the word the verse gives us, so mourning is the one that fits the blank.
Hiding is a fair guess, friend, but these verses never say it. Mark 16:10 says they were “…mourning and weeping.” That's grief, plain and simple. The blank is looking for mourning.
It's the other way around, friend. Verse 11 says, “…they did not believe it.” Mary told them Jesus was alive and that she had seen Him, and they still didn't believe. So the answer here is False.
Right, false. Mark 16:11 says, “…they did not believe it.” Mary tells them He's alive and that she has seen Him, and still they don't believe it. Not a quick yes anywhere in that verse.

True. Mark says Jesus “…appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked along in the country.” Mark doesn't tell us what that different form looked like, so I'm not going to make something up. I'll stick to what's in the verse, and it's plenty.

It's actually true, friend. Verse 12 says Jesus “…appeared in a different form to two of them…” That's what Mark tells us, and he doesn't describe the form. So I'll leave that part where Mark leaves it.

explanations.answer: They do not believe them either
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 13 says, “…they did not believe them either.” Mary's report wasn't believed, and now the two from the country get the same treatment. Two reports, and neither one is believed. That's a tough crowd, friend.

explanations.answer: They run out to find Jesus
explanations.explanation: I wish I could give you that ending, but Mark doesn't write it. Verse 13 says, “…they did not believe them either.” The word “either” tells us the report from the two got the same reception Mary's did. Running out to find Jesus isn't in this verse.
A big group celebration would be a nice scene, but it's not in these verses. Verse 13 says, “…they did not believe them either.” The report from the two goes over the same way Mary's did.

explanations.answer: Their unbelief and hardness of heart
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus “…rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart…” (Mark 16:14). Not fun to hear, and I've been scolded by a burnt tray myself. Still, notice that He appears to them while they're eating. He comes to the Eleven Himself.

That one happened in Gethsemane, the garden where Jesus prayed. He came back and found them sleeping (Mark 14:37). It's a different moment, though. Here in Mark 16:14, the rebuke is for “…their unbelief and hardness of heart…”

explanations.answer: Arguing about who was the greatest
explanations.explanation: The disciples did argue about who was the greatest, back on the road (Mark 9:34). That's a different moment, friend. The rebuke in Mark 16:14 is for “…their unbelief and hardness of heart…” This time the problem is believing, not rank.

explanations.answer: Those who had seen Him after He rose
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Mark says the rebuke was “…because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen.” That means the people who had seen Him, like Mary and the two from the country. The Eleven heard from eyewitnesses and didn't believe them.

explanations.answer: The prophets who wrote about Him long ago
explanations.explanation: The prophets aren't named in this verse, friend. Mark 16:14 gives the reason for the rebuke: “…because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen.” The ones not believed are people who had seen Him alive.

explanations.answer: The angel who spoke at the empty tomb
explanations.explanation: No angel gets named in this verse. Mark says the Eleven were rebuked “…because they did not believe those who had seen Him after He had risen.” Those words point to people who had seen Jesus alive. That's who they didn't believe.
World is right. Jesus says, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.” That's a big territory, friend. I stay on one little planet and still struggle to cover it with cookies.

A city would be a nice route, but it's not what Jesus says. He says, “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.” (Mark 16:15). That reaches a lot farther than one city. The blank wants “world.”

A temple is one building, friend. Jesus' words in Mark 16:15 are “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.” So He sends them out, and He points at the whole world, not one place. That's the word the blank wants.
That's what He says. “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved…” (Mark 16:16). Two things go together there: believing and being baptized. Jesus just states it plainly.
Feasts don't come up in verse 16, friend. Jesus says, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved…” That's the one He names. The answer is believing and being baptized.

Jesus doesn't point to where anyone was born. He says, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved…” (Mark 16:16). Remember that He had just told them to preach to “every creature” in verse 15. So the message goes out wide, and the answer is believing and being baptized.
True. Jesus says, “…whoever does not believe will be condemned.” (Mark 16:16). That's a heavy line, friend, and I won't joke about it. It's why this message matters so much.

It's actually true. Right after promising salvation, Jesus says, “…whoever does not believe will be condemned.” (Mark 16:16). That's a heavy line, and I won't joke about it. Both halves are in the same verse.
That's number one on the list. Jesus says, “In My name they will drive out demons…” (Mark 16:17). Notice the words “In My name…” This one comes first, and the rest of the list follows.
Raising the dead isn't on Jesus' list in verses 17 and 18, friend. The first sign He names is “In My name they will drive out demons…” That's the one that leads off. The rest come after it.
Calling down fire isn't in this list. In Mark 16:17, the first sign Jesus names is “In My name they will drive out demons…” Everything else on the list comes after that one.

True. Jesus says, “they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be made well.” (Mark 16:18). This one is a promise to believers, and Jesus says it plainly. It sits right there in His list of signs.
It's actually true, friend. Mark 16:18 says, “they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will be made well.” Jesus puts that on the list with the other signs. He says it right out.

explanations.answer: At the right hand of God
explanations.explanation: Yes. Mark says Jesus “…was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.” (Mark 16:19). That's where the story of Jesus' time with them ends. He is taken up, and then He sits down.
Angels don't come up in verse 19, friend. Mark says Jesus “…was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.” That's the seat He takes. The text names God's right hand.

Moses and Elijah did appear with Jesus on a mountain, talking with Him (Mark 9:4). That was a different moment, friend. In Mark 16:19, Jesus “…was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.”

That's what Mark says. “And they went out and preached everywhere…” (Mark 16:20). Jesus gave them the job, and they went and did it. The same group that hadn't believed the news is now out spreading it.

Staying hidden would be a quiet way to end it, friend, but that's not what Mark writes. Verse 20 says, “And they went out and preached everywhere…” In verse 15 Jesus tells them to go into all the world, and here they are doing it.
Going back to fishing isn't anywhere in these verses. Mark 16:20 says, “And they went out and preached everywhere…” Jesus gave them the job in verse 15, and this is them doing it.
It's the opposite, friend. Mark 16:20 says, “…the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.” So they weren't out there alone. No solo baking for these folks.
Right, false. Mark says, “…the Lord worked through them, confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it.” (Mark 16:20). They go out, and the Lord works through them. They aren't on their own.
